title: Valid consent
blurb: What makes consent valid, the three types, how the process should run, and what to do when a patient hesitates, refuses or wants to stop.
question: A patient signed a consent form for an extraction last week. Today, as the dentist picks up the forceps, she says 'I'm not sure about this any more' and looks tearful. Is her consent still valid, and what should happen next?

teach.body: Consent is a patient's permission for an examination or treatment. GDC Principle 3 says you must obtain valid consent before starting treatment, and treating without it can be unlawful. Consent is not a form or a signature: it is the patient's genuine, informed decision. It applies to the specific treatment discussed, and it continues throughout the appointment. The clinician carrying out the treatment is responsible for obtaining it. The nurse supports the process and watches for signs that consent is slipping.

letters.sub: Given freely, with no pressure from staff, family or anyone else
Options (including doing nothing), risks, benefits, costs, and time to decide
The person can understand, retain, weigh up and communicate the decision

teach.caption: Miss any one and consent isn't valid. Since the Montgomery ruling (2015), patients must be told about material risks: those a reasonable person in their position would think significant, and any this patient would particularly care about.
A signature is evidence that a discussion happened. It is not the consent itself.

steps.label: Explain
steps.sub: Options, risks, benefits and costs, in plain language

steps.label: Check understanding
steps.sub: Answer questions; use an interpreter if needed

steps.label: Give time
steps.sub: No rushing; time to think about bigger decisions

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: What was discussed, the decision and how it was obtained

teach.caption: Rushed or skipped conversations are a common cause of consent problems.

teach.body: A patient can withdraw consent at any time, even after signing. If they want to stop, the dentist stops as soon as it is safe, for example after placing a temporary dressing, rather than leaving a tooth half-prepared. If a patient hesitates, looks distressed or says they don't understand, pause and tell the dentist so the options can be discussed again. A refusal must be respected: explain the consequences, accept the decision and record it, so it is clear the choice was informed.

children.label: Brief rest
children.sub: Check they're happy to go on

teach.body: Refer questions about risks or clinical choices to the clinician rather than answering yourself. Help overcome barriers: arrange a professional interpreter for limited English, and read a form aloud for a patient who struggles to read, checking understanding and recording how consent was obtained. If you witness a signature, you confirm that the named person signed it. If you witness that a treatment plan was given, check the patient received it and had the chance to ask questions.

teach.text: A signed form is not the same as valid consent. If the patient now says they don't understand, or want to stop, the signature counts for nothing. What they say today overrides what they signed last week.

items: Valid consent: voluntary, informed (options, risks, costs, time) and given by someone with capacity.
Types: implied (actions), verbal (spoken) and written (signed); record all of them.
Process: explain, check understanding, give time, agree, record.
Consent can be withdrawn at any time: stop at a safe point; pause if the patient hesitates.
Refer clinical questions to the clinician; record refusals as well as agreement.

summary: You can now state the three conditions for valid consent, tell implied, verbal and written consent apart, describe a sound consent process, and act correctly when a patient hesitates, refuses, doesn't understand or wants to stop.

A.q: Which statement best describes valid consent in dental care?
options: Voluntary, informed and given with capacity
A signed form from any adult present
Agreement renewed once each year at recall
Permission from the patient's next of kin
A.why: Valid consent must be voluntary, informed and given by a person with capacity to make the decision.

whyNot.1: A signature alone doesn't prove the patient understood or chose freely.
whyNot.2: Consent is specific to the treatment and ongoing, not an annual formality.
whyNot.3: Next of kin can't consent for an adult who has capacity.

A.q: A patient nods and opens their mouth after the dentist explains a routine examination. What type of consent is this?
options: Written consent
Verbal consent
Implied consent
Presumed consent
A.why: Implied consent is shown by actions, such as opening the mouth after an explanation.

whyNot.3: 'Presumed consent' isn't a valid basis for dental treatment.

A.q: A patient becomes distressed partway through a filling and asks the dentist to stop. What must happen?
options: Finish quickly, since consent was given
Stop immediately, mid-preparation
Ask the patient to sign a refusal first
Stop at the earliest safe point
A.why: Consent can be withdrawn at any time. The dentist stops as soon as it is safe, for example after placing a temporary dressing.

whyNot.0: Earlier consent doesn't override a withdrawal.
whyNot.1: Leaving a tooth open mid-preparation could harm the patient; stop at a safe point.

B.q: A patient asks you about the risks of their planned root canal treatment. What is the best response?
options: Refer the question to the clinician
Explain the risks in your own words
Tell them the risks are very small
Give them a leaflet instead
B.why: Information about clinical risks must come from the clinician, who is responsible for consent.

whyNot.1: You might give incomplete or wrong information about risk.
whyNot.2: Reassuring without knowledge could mislead the patient.
whyNot.3: A leaflet can help, but it doesn't replace the clinician answering their question.

B.q: A patient is hesitating about an extraction. Which behaviour most undermines voluntary consent?
options: Offering time to think it over
Explaining what happens if they wait
Telling them they have no choice
Asking what is worrying them
B.why: Pressure, such as saying they have no choice, means consent is no longer voluntary.

whyNot.0: Giving time supports a free decision.
whyNot.1: Explaining consequences is part of informed consent.
whyNot.3: Exploring worries supports the patient's decision.

B.q: A patient with limited English attends alone for an extraction. What best supports informed consent?
options: Proceed if the patient nods along
Ask another patient who speaks it to translate
Speak slowly and loudly in English
Use a professional interpreter
B.why: A professional interpreter ensures the patient genuinely understands the options and risks.

whyNot.1: Another patient isn't trained and it breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.2: Volume doesn't overcome a language barrier.

C.q: Which sequence best reflects a sound consent process for planned treatment?
options: Agree, explain, record, then answer questions
Record, explain, then agree
Explain, answer questions, agree, record
Explain, start treatment, then record
C.why: Explain the options and risks, answer questions, obtain agreement, then record the discussion and decision.

whyNot.0: Agreement before explanation can't be informed.
whyNot.1: You can't record a decision before it's been made.
whyNot.3: Agreement must come before treatment starts.

C.q: A patient refuses a radiograph the dentist has recommended. What should happen?
options: Take it anyway, as it's in their interest
Explain the reasons, respect and record it
Ask a relative to persuade them to have it
Refuse to carry on seeing the patient at all
C.why: A patient with capacity can refuse. Explain why it was recommended and the consequences, respect the decision and record it.

whyNot.0: Taking a radiograph without consent is not allowed.
whyNot.2: Using family to pressure them undermines voluntary consent.
whyNot.3: Refusing one item doesn't end their care; other options may exist.

C.q: You are asked to witness a patient's signature on a consent form. What does witnessing confirm?
options: The signature was made by the named person
The treatment chosen is clinically right
The patient will not later change their mind
The dentist explained every single risk
C.why: A witness confirms that the person named on the form is the one who signed it.

whyNot.1: Clinical judgement is the dentist's, not the witness's.
whyNot.2: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, whatever was signed.
whyNot.3: The witness confirms the signature, not the full content of the discussion.

reteach.title: Consent is a conversation, not a form
reteach.question: Think of consent as a green light that the patient controls. What turns it green, and what can turn it red at any moment?

blocks.body: The light turns green only when the patient has heard the options and risks, had their questions answered, felt free to choose and is able to decide. Paperwork just records that the light was green at that moment. The patient can flick it to amber ('I'm not sure') or red ('stop') whenever they like. Your job is to watch the light: notice hesitation, tears, a raised hand or a puzzled face, and make sure the dentist sees it too.

bands.label: Wants to stop: stop at a safe point

blocks.text: Silence or a nod is not the same as understanding, especially with anxiety, hearing loss or limited English. Check understanding out loud.

explain.body: Consent must be freely given, without pressure from staff, family or anyone else. Time pressure and 'you have no choice' both undermine it.

options: It is signed in front of an independent witness
It is given without pressure from anyone
It is given by someone over 18
It is recorded in the notes
test.why: Voluntary means the patient chose freely, without pressure from staff, family or others.

whyNot.0: A witness confirms a signature, not freedom of choice.
whyNot.2: Age relates to capacity, not voluntariness.
whyNot.3: Recording documents consent; it doesn't make it voluntary.

explain.body: The patient needs the options (including no treatment), risks, benefits and costs in plain language, with time to consider. Questions about risk go to the clinician.

test.q: A patient is given a plan with several options and costs. What best supports an informed decision?
options: Recommend the cheapest option to them as best
Ask them to decide before they leave
Give them the form to sign and post back
Explain options, risks and costs; give time
test.why: Informed consent needs clear information about options, risks and costs, plus time to consider.

whyNot.0: Cost alone isn't the basis of an informed choice.
whyNot.1: Rushing a decision undermines informed consent.
whyNot.2: A form at home without discussion doesn't inform them.

explain.body: Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Stop at a safe point, pause if the patient is unsure, and record discussions, decisions and refusals.

test.q: A patient signs a form but then says they don't understand the procedure. What is the best action?
options: Proceed, since the form is signed
Pause so the dentist can explain
Ask them to sign the form again
Cancel all future treatment
test.why: Without understanding, consent isn't informed. Pause so the clinician can explain further before anything continues.

whyNot.0: A signature doesn't make consent valid if they don't understand.
whyNot.2: Signing again doesn't fix the lack of understanding.
whyNot.3: That's an overreaction; they just need more explanation.
